content: Drospirenone and Ethinyl estradiol is a contraceptive medication approved by the FDA for the treatment of premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), acne, and contraception. Common side effects include headaches or migraines, menstrual irregularities, nausea or vomiting, breast pain or tenderness, and mood changes. For the treatment of moderate acne vulgaris in women aged 14 years or older who have no contraindications to oral contraceptive therapy and have achieved menarche, a dose of 0.02 mg is recommended. This dose should only be used for acne treatment if the patient also desires oral contraception for birth control. Additionally, 0.02 mg is indicated for use in women to prevent pregnancy. Dosing Instructions for Nikki: Take one tablet orally at the same time every day. Missing pills or taking them incorrectly may increase the failure rate. To maximize contraceptive effectiveness, Nikki must be taken exactly as directed, in the order specified on the package. If a single pill is missed, it should be taken as soon as remembered. Starting Nikki: 1. Day 1 Start: Begin taking one pink Nikki tablet daily on the first day of the menstrual cycle (Day 1 of menstruation). Continue taking one pink tablet daily for 24 consecutive days, followed by one white inert tablet daily on Days 25 through 28. Nikki should be taken in the order directed on the package, preferably at the same time each day, after an evening meal or at bedtime with liquid if needed. Nikki can be taken with or without food. If Nikki is started later than the first day of the menstrual cycle, it will not be effective as a contraceptive until after the first 7 consecutive days of administration. During this time, a non-hormonal contraceptive should be used as a backup. Consider the possibility of ovulation and conception prior to starting the medication. 2. Sunday Start: Begin taking one pink Nikki tablet daily on the first Sunday after the onset of menstruation. Follow the same regimen as above. Nikki will not be effective as a contraceptive until after the first 7 consecutive days of administration, and a non-hormonal contraceptive should be used as a backup during this time. The patient should begin her next and all subsequent 28-day regimens of Nikki on the same day of the week as the first regimen, following the same schedule. She should start taking her pink tablets the day after ingesting the last white tablet, regardless of whether a menstrual period has occurred or is still in progress. If a subsequent cycle of Nikki is started later than the day following the last white tablet, another method of contraception should be used until she has taken a pink Nikki tablet daily for seven consecutive days. Switching to Nikki: From another birth control pill: Start Nikki on the same day a new pack of the previous oral contraceptive would have been started. From a transdermal patch or vaginal ring: Start Nikki when the next application would have been due. From an injection: Start Nikki when the next dose would have been due. From an intrauterine contraceptive or implant: Start Nikki on the day of removal. Missed Pills: If one or more active pink tablets are missed, the risk of pregnancy increases. Follow the instructions in the What to Do if You Miss Pills section of the FDA-approved patient labeling. Breakthrough bleeding following missed tablets is usually transient and of no consequence. If one or more white tablets are missed, the patient should still be protected against pregnancy provided she begins taking a new cycle of pink tablets on the proper day. Postpartum Use: For postpartum women who do not breastfeed or after a second-trimester abortion, start Nikki no earlier than 4 weeks postpartum due to the increased risk of thromboembolism. If the patient starts Nikki postpartum and has not yet had a period, evaluate for possible pregnancy and instruct her to use an additional method of contraception until she has taken Nikki for 7 consecutive days. Gastrointestinal Disturbances: In cases of severe vomiting or diarrhea, absorption may not be complete, and additional contraceptive measures should be taken. If vomiting occurs within 3 to 4 hours after taking a tablet, it should be regarded as a missed tablet. Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD): The recommended dose for PMDD is one active (pink) Yaz® tablet orally every day for 24 consecutive days, followed by one inert (white) tablet daily for 4 days per menstrual cycle. Therapy should start either on the first day of the menstrual period or on the first Sunday after the onset of menstruation. Efficacy for PMDD has not been assessed beyond three menstrual cycles. Contraindications: Do not prescribe Nikki to women with the following conditions: Renal impairment Adrenal insufficiency High risk of arterial or venous thrombotic diseases (e.g., smokers over age 35, history of deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism, cerebrovascular disease, coronary artery disease, thrombotic valvular or rhythm diseases, inherited or acquired hypercoagulopathies, uncontrolled hypertension, diabetes mellitus with vascular disease, migraines with aura in women over age 35) Undiagnosed abnormal uterine bleeding Breast cancer or other estrogenor progestin-sensitive cancers Liver tumors or liver disease Pregnancy Warnings: Thromboembolic Disorders: Discontinue Nikki if an arterial or venous thrombotic event occurs. Drospirenone-containing COCs may have a higher risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) compared to other progestins. The risk of VTE is highest during the first year of use and decreases after discontinuation. Hyperkalemia: Drospirenone has antimineralocorticoid activity and may increase serum potassium levels in high-risk patients. Monitor serum potassium during the first treatment cycle in women taking medications that may increase potassium levels. Breast and Reproductive Organ Carcinoma: Women with current or past breast cancer should not use Nikki. While some studies suggest an increased risk of cervical cancer with COC use, this may be influenced by other factors such as sexual behavior. Liver Disease: Discontinue Nikki if jaundice develops. Hepatic adenomas and hepatocellular carcinoma have been associated with long-term COC use. Hypertension: Monitor blood pressure in women with controlled hypertension and discontinue Nikki if blood pressure rises significantly. Women with uncontrolled hypertension or hypertension with vascular disease should not use COCs. Gallbladder Disease: COC use may slightly increase the risk of gallbladder disease. Carbohydrate and Lipid Metabolism: Monitor prediabetic and diabetic women taking Nikki, as COCs may decrease glucose tolerance. This information is intended for healthcare professionals to guide safe and effective use of Drospirenone and Ethinyl estradiol.
